svg.text: The Cupcake Audit — is the cafe's "200 calories" claim believable?
A cafe claims its cupcakes average 200 cal. You buy one a day for 10 days, weigh the calories, and put the claim on trial. Built in R · theme: gold & teal.

text.tspan: You suspect the cupcakes are bigger than
claimed. A hunch is not proof, so you
collect data
: one cupcake per day for 10 days.
We compare ONE sample of
numbers to ONE fixed value
chosen before seeing data.
It answers: is a sample mean far enough from a
fixed reference value to doubt that value?
Same family of test if the reference is a target,
a regulation, a historical value, or a label claim.

svg.text: Two means? That's a two-sample t-test. Paired? Paired t-test. Here: one.

g.text: true (unknown) mean of all the cafe's cupcakes
the claimed value we test against = 200
standard error = s/√n, the wiggle of the mean

svg.text: 4 · THE DATA — is 214.4 far from 200, or just noise?
The 10 values: 198 246 188 218 254 203 206 202 210 219. Mean x̄ = 214.4 sits above the claim. But baking is messy.
The real question: is the 14.4-cal gap big compared with ordinary cupcake-to-cupcake variation? The mean is on trial — not one dramatic cupcake.
s = 20.9 says cupcakes vary a lot. The claim fixes the
center but not the spread, so we estimate spread from
the sample, then turn it into the standard error next.
H₀ (null) — give the cafe the benefit of the doubt
the true mean really is the claim
label may be wrong either way
Why two-sided? We suspected "higher", but a fair test
allows surprise in either direction. We test H₀ and ask:
how surprising is our data if H₀ were true?
7 · THE NULL WORLD — "if the claim is true, cupcakes vary around 200"

text.tspan: Under H₀, single cupcakes still
scatter widely. Even a high one
can be ordinary baking noise.
We judge the average, not
any one cupcake.

svg.text: each dot = one cupcake under the null
8 · STANDARD ERROR — spread of the mean

text.tspan: Individual cupcakes vary by s = 20.9. But the
average of 10 is far more stable than one cupcake.
If the true mean were 200, sample means from
groups of 10 would typically wiggle around 200 by
about 6.6 calories — that is our measuring stick.

svg.text: 9 · ONE CUPCAKE vs THE MEAN OF TEN — same center, different spread
10 · THE t-STATISTIC — the gap measured in SEs
Convert the 14.4-cal gap into "how many standard errors". That standardized distance is t.
We use the t-distribution (not z) because the spread s was estimated from a small sample. Small n → fatter tails.
11 · THE p-VALUE — how often would |t| ≥ 2.18 happen if H₀ were true?
the time if the claim were true.
13 · THE VERDICT — suspicious, not enough to convict
Since p = 0.0575 > 0.05, we do not reject H₀ at the 5% level. The 95% CI still includes 200, so 200 stays plausible.
Ten cupcakes are simply too few, given this much variation, to rule out ordinary noise.
14 · COLLECT MORE — n = 30 sharpens the evidence (power)
t.test(cup30, mu = 200) → t = 3.08, df = 29, p = 0.0045. Mean barely changed (213.4), but SE shrank, so now the CI clears 200.
Power lesson: more data shrinks SE, so the same size of difference becomes easier to detect. Never report "not significant" as "no effect".
⚠ Choose the direction BEFORE seeing the data, or it's cheating.
16 · THE FULL CHAIN — claim to verdict
A one-sample t-test compares a sample mean to a fixed external value. Ten cupcakes looked suspicious; thirty cupcakes, with less uncertainty, made the case.
